The Sketching Gap: Rethinking Sketch AI Through Illustration Practice

Zeynep Begüm Kara, Tevfik Metin Sezgin

Koç University, Istanbul, Türkiye

Paper

Figure 1. (a) Share of papers by the role the sketch plays in the system, three-year moving average. (b) Papers in each role linked to practice-related uses. Abstract

Computational research has developed many ways of working with sketches, from recognising and retrieving them to generating, transforming and modelling visual material. Yet what a system can do with a sketch does not necessarily account for the roles sketches play within established creative and professional workflows. We introduce the term Sketching Gap for the relation between how computational research makes sketches operational and how sketches function within situated practice. In this article, we examine this gap through illustration.

Drawing on illustration literature, we consider how sketches become useful within an unfolding practice, including how they support developing work, remain provisional, return later, and move between people. We then analyse a corpus of computational sketch research published between 2011 and 2026 to examine how computational systems position sketches and how these roles relate to those found in illustration practice. This comparison shifts attention from isolated computational capabilities to the roles those capabilities take within longer processes of making. The Sketching Gap therefore opens a space for examining how computational capabilities and situated sketching practices can inform and extend one another.

Method

Each paper was read in full by Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. In a first task, the model answered short questions about what the system does with a sketch and how people work with it, quoting a supporting passage for every answer. In a second task, papers that met the basic condition for an illustration perspective received one further question about how the system actually uses that feature. Every question was asked three times and the most frequent answer kept; the three answers were identical for 93% of answers. An evaluation was counted as involving people only when its passage mentioned human participants. A researcher coded a random sample of 50 papers and reviewed each against the model's answers and passages; agreement on the codes used in the analysis was 92% (mean Cohen's κ = 0.83).

Sketch AI at a Glance

Each grid shows the 2,087 papers as 100 dots, one dot for roughly one per cent. Hover over a category to highlight it.

Sketch AI through five illustration perspectives

Share of Sketch AI papers in each task that connect with five ways sketches take part in illustration practice.

Five Illustration Perspectives

The perspectives come from writing on illustration practice. Each describes a way in which sketches take part in illustration. For every perspective we asked which Sketch AI systems connect with it, and then what kind of relation they establish.

Data

The coded dataset, with every answer and the passage quoted from each paper, is available upon request.

Prompts

The coding used two tasks. Task 1 has two parts, run as two prompts: Task 1a describes what the system does with a sketch, and Task 1b how people work with it. Task 2 is a single prompt that asks only the follow-up questions for the perspectives a paper connects with. Inside the prompts, these are labelled Task A, Task B and Task C.
